$comment: Scotland, Contract Law - the statutory personal-bar mechanism that can excuse a missing formal writing requirement for land contracts, and its narrow judicial construction. Scots law genuinely does not require consideration for a binding contract, unlike English law - this entry covers a different but equally distinctive feature: the formal writing requirement for land transactions and its escape valve.

authorities.name: Requirements of Writing (Scotland) Act 1995, s.1
authorities.date_note: Enactment year. The text verified this session is the current in-force version.
authorities.proposition: Writing is not generally required for the constitution of a contract, unilateral obligation, or trust (s.1(1)) - Scots law does not require consideration, unlike English law, but a written document complying with s.2 is required for a contract creating, transferring, varying, or extinguishing an interest in land (s.1(2)(a)(i)). Where such a land contract lacks the required writing, but one party has acted in reliance on it with the other's knowledge and acquiescence and would be materially prejudiced by withdrawal, the other party cannot withdraw and the contract is not invalid for want of writing (s.1(3)-(4)). Subsections (3) and (4) replace the former common-law rules of rei interventus and homologation (s.1(5)).
authorities.verification_note: Fetched live and directly this session, on two independent passes, word-for-word consistent both times.

authorities.name: The Advice Centre for Mortgages Ltd v McNicoll
authorities.proposition: The statutory personal bar in s.1(3)-(4) operates as a shield, not a sword: it prevents withdrawal from a contract but confers no positive claim, and it binds only the original contracting parties, not singular successors (such as a purchaser who took the land after the original party failed to formalise a lease). It applies only to contracts creating purely personal rights under s.1(2)(a), not to deeds intended to create real rights under s.1(2)(b) that are perfected by registration or taking possession. Section 1(5) abolished the common-law doctrine of rei interventus 'in its entirety,' including its older use to prove that consensus had been reached at all (not merely its use to cure a missing signature) - overruling the practical effect of Errol v Walker 1966 SC 93 (not independently verified in this file).

Outer House decision, recorded as PERSUASIVE authority weight.

edges.verified_via: McNicoll [2006] CSOH 58, paras 17-18, 22, 30, per the researching agent's browser-session read of BAILII: construes s.1(3)-(5)'s personal bar narrowly, confining it to personal-right contracts between the original parties and confirming its total replacement of rei interventus and homologation.

what_this_is_not: Two nodes covering the personal-bar escape valve for informal land contracts. Does not cover offer/acceptance formation generally, the Contract (Scotland) Act 1997's rectification provisions, promise as a distinct unilateral obligation, or any other Scots Contract Law subject - all remain unbuilt.
